title: Measure security boundaries and residual authority
purpose: Help developers and security practitioners explain what controls prevent, detect and still permit in a trading application, then measure what those protections cost. Learn in phases before comparing runtime products or platform alternatives.
entryAssumptions: C3 normal trading and its Kubernetes runtime are understood; no production data is used.
concepts: A reachable destination is not unlimited database authority; scoped service authority is not end-user business authorization.
An alert or killed process does not prove that impact was prevented.
A compensating control must meet the same security objective and preserve business correctness; fewer application code lines or faster requests alone do not establish an equivalent boundary.
Security cost depends on the path: request latency, committed settlement and visible notifications are different outcomes, and moving work to a proxy or asynchronous queue does not remove its cost.
runtimePrerequisites: The integrated state is planned. Prototype onboarding is explicitly limited to its verified host and fixture scope; run only one full cluster at a time.

transitions.motivation: A working application does not yet explain its security boundaries.
transitions.increment: Add staged controls, bounded experiments, independent outcome evidence and a method for comparing security cost.
transitions.evidence: Positive trading plus attributable negative checks and residual-authority outcomes in the same pinned deployment; matched-workload cost measurements before crediting an alternative control.

after: Target: learners can reproduce layered security, explain residual risk and evaluate security/cost tradeoffs; integrated acceptance and performance measurements are pending.

objectives.outcome: Explain which security layer intervened using correlated decisions and independent state evidence.
Distinguish denied out-of-grant operations from residual misuse of legitimate service authority, then compare detection with prevention.
Reproduce a bounded experiment, restore synthetic data and verify that legitimate trading continues within a measured resource budget.

Compare a control and a proposed replacement against the same security and business-correctness outcomes, using per-path p95/p99 latency, throughput, resource use and operating effort to justify retaining, replacing, combining or deferring them.

walkthrough.action: Planned integrated walkthrough: predict a decision, run positive and negative controls, inspect effects, compare runtime modes and reset. Prototype checkpoint evidence is available separately.
walkthrough.expected: Attribute each decision and resulting state; do not infer prevention from an alert or claim a fixture is integrated.

walkthrough.action: Planned exercise after cumulative baseline acceptance: choose one path, such as order submission through committed settlement, and predict the cost of its controls. Declare workload and trading-owner budgets, collect repeated baseline measurements, then evaluate a separately gated alternative against identical security and correctness checks. Keep operator lookup, reads and asynchronous notification timings distinct. A service-mesh comparison belongs to the separate follow-on, not this baseline implementation.
walkthrough.expected: An evidence-backed decision joins the intervening layer and final SQL/message effects with p95/p99 latency, throughput, errors/queues, CPU/memory and whole-system operating effort. Report sample counts and uncertainty. Record unmeasured or incomplete results explicitly; a mesh reducing code or overhead remains a hypothesis until tested.

assessments.question: A service talks to its allowed database and a runtime alert fires. What proves prevention and successful recovery?
assessments.guidance: Inspect independent canary and downstream effects after settling, compare the same inputs across profiles, reset and rerun positive trading; record resource costs and limitations.

assessments.question: A proposed service mesh removes application TLS configuration and improves average response time. What evidence would justify it as a replacement or compensating control, and what responsibility might still belong to the application?
assessments.guidance: Compare the same pinned workload, identities, threats, failure cases and independent business outcomes, including cancellation, replay and within-grant misuse. Keep account authorization unless the candidate actually receives and enforces that context. Compare per-path p95/p99 and settlement latency, throughput, errors/queues, CPU/memory and proxy/control-plane resource use, plus setup, rotation, debugging and upgrade effort. Record sample counts, uncertainty, residual risk and an accountable retain/replace/combine/defer decision against declared budgets. Current measurements are absent and budgets are unspecified; no efficiency or equivalent-protection claim is yet justified.

limitations: Planned generated state; current evidence covers individual checkpoints and candidate integrations only.
CVE/OSERA is optional and planned; CALM is a separate successor. Local checks are not compliance certification.

Per-path performance and operating costs are unmeasured, and trading-owner latency/availability budgets are not yet declared. Service-mesh or ingress savings are hypotheses for a separate follow-on comparison; neither that comparison nor CALM is required to finish the manually established baseline.

coaching.diagnosticQuestion: Which identity and authority does each boundary actually enforce?
coaching.predictionPrompt: Predict whether a within-grant write by a compromised service will be distinguishable from normal work.
hints: Follow the identity from the user through the process and database role.
Inspect final state independently; an alert is a separate observation.
coaching.misconception: Strong networking or a runtime alert guarantees that all business-unauthorized writes are prevented.
coaching.evidenceToRequest: Pinned configuration, correlated decisions, independent before/after outcomes, reset evidence and continued trading.

coaching.diagnosticQuestion: Where does a request wait before its business effect is committed, and which component has enough identity context to authorize that effect?
coaching.predictionPrompt: Predict which cost a gateway or service mesh might remove, move or add, and which account-level decision it cannot make from workload identity alone.
hints: Draw one complete request-to-effect path before selecting timing points; include queues and asynchronous work.
Replay the same load and negative scenarios, count unsuccessful work, and compare tail latency with independent final state.
Count proxy and control-plane resources and operating effort alongside application code removed; keep an unmeasured result unknown.
coaching.misconception: A service mesh with less application code and a lower average latency necessarily provides equivalent security at lower total cost.
coaching.evidenceToRequest: Pinned baseline/candidate configurations, identical security and business-correctness results, matched-load per-path p95/p99 with sample counts and uncertainty, whole-system resource and operating costs, declared budgets and a decision documenting residual risk.
